title: Primitive type
body:
Four names for the same thing, which is worth knowing before a textbook switches on you
mid-chapter:

| Name | Where you see it |
|---|---|
| **Atomic type** | this course's wording, and what the notes use |
| **Primitive type** | Java, C#, most language documentation |
| **Built-in type** | compiler and standard-library docs |
| **Fundamental type** | the C++ standard itself |

All four mean a type the language provides directly, holding exactly one value, with no
internal structure you can reach into: `int`, `double`, `float`, `char`, `bool`. The
opposite is a [[Compound type]], which holds many values under one name
([[Array]], [[Structure]], [[C-String]]).

The distinction that actually bites is not the name, it is what a variable of that type
*is*. A primitive variable holds its value directly, so assignment copies the value and
[[Call by value]] means the function gets its own copy. A compound or pointer variable
holds a location, so copying it copies the reference and you can end up with two names
for one piece of memory.

Full treatment lives in
[[Atomic type]].
See also [[Data type]] for the list, and [[Data representation]] in
[[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] for what these actually look like in bits.
